questions.prompt: What does a single perceptron compute?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function

A perceptron multiplies each input by a weight, adds a bias, and applies an activation function to the result — the same basic building block used throughout neural networks.
keyPoints: A perceptron multiplies each input by a weight, adds a bias, and applies an activation function to the result — the same basic building block used throughout neural networks.

questions.prompt: If you stack multiple layers with no activation function between them, what happens mathematically?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The entire stack collapses into a single equivalent linear transformation, no matter how many layers there are

Composing linear transformations (matrix multiplications plus bias) always produces another linear transformation — stacking purely linear layers, regardless of how many, is mathematically equivalent to one linear layer.
keyPoints: Composing linear transformations (matrix multiplications plus bias) always produces another linear transformation — stacking purely linear layers, regardless of how many, is mathematically equivalent to one linear layer.

questions.prompt: What does Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) use for each weight update, compared to plain gradient descent on the whole dataset?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A small random mini-batch of the training data

SGD updates weights using small random mini-batches rather than the full dataset at once, which speeds up training and introduces some helpful randomness into the optimization process.
keyPoints: SGD updates weights using small random mini-batches rather than the full dataset at once, which speeds up training and introduces some helpful randomness into the optimization process.

questions.prompt: What does dropout do during training?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: It randomly zeroes out a fraction of neurons at each training step, forcing more robust, redundant representations

By randomly disabling different neurons on each training step, dropout prevents the network from relying too heavily on any single neuron, encouraging it to spread useful information across many neurons instead.
keyPoints: By randomly disabling different neurons on each training step, dropout prevents the network from relying too heavily on any single neuron, encouraging it to spread useful information across many neurons instead.

questions.prompt: Why is feeding a full image directly into a large fully-connected layer impractical?
questions.referenceAnswer: A modest image has well over 100,000 pixel values — connecting all of them to even a modest number of neurons creates millions of weights in a single layer, which is both expensive to train and very likely to overfit.
keyPoints: A modest image has well over 100,000 pixel values — connecting all of them to even a modest number of neurons creates millions of weights in a single layer, which is both expensive to train and very likely to overfit.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind transfer learning?
questions.referenceAnswer: Transfer learning reuses the general-purpose knowledge already captured by a network trained on a large dataset, adapting it to a new task rather than learning everything again from zero.
keyPoints: Transfer learning reuses the general-purpose knowledge already captured by a network trained on a large dataset, adapting it to a new task rather than learning everything again from zero.

Using only fully-connected layers instead of convolutional ones

questions.prompt: What is the vanishing gradient problem in the context of plain RNNs?
questions.referenceAnswer: Because gradients are computed by repeated multiplication across time steps, they can shrink dramatically over long sequences in a plain RNN, making it difficult for information from early steps to meaningfully influence learning at much later steps.
keyPoints: Because gradients are computed by repeated multiplication across time steps, they can shrink dramatically over long sequences in a plain RNN, making it difficult for information from early steps to meaningfully influence learning at much later steps.

questions.prompt: What are the two networks in a GAN, and what does each try to do?
questions.referenceAnswer: GANs pit a generator (which creates fake examples) against a discriminator (which tries to tell real examples from generated fakes) — this adversarial competition is the core training mechanism.
keyPoints: GANs pit a generator (which creates fake examples) against a discriminator (which tries to tell real examples from generated fakes) — this adversarial competition is the core training mechanism.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Inspect learning rate and activation statistics before increasing model size. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Inspect learning rate and activation statistics before increasing model size.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Try to overfit a tiny batch. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Try to overfit a tiny batch.
Measure a representative workload.
